meta.title: How a Car Insurance Claim Works — Safe House Insurance
meta.desc: What happens after you report a car insurance claim: who decides fault, what your deductible really costs, how long each step takes, total loss, rental cars, and the mistakes that make a claim harder. Safe House Insurance, El Paso TX.

hero.h1: How a car insurance claim works, from the crash to the cheque
hero.lede:
Who decides fault, what your deductible actually costs you, how long each
        step takes, what a total loss means, and the handful of mistakes that make a claim
        harder than it needed to be. Written by licensed agents in El Paso who do this daily.

key.l1:
Report it the same day if you can. "Promptly" in a policy is not a number of
          days — it is however long the evidence lasts.
key.l2:
Reporting is not the same as claiming. Telling your carrier what happened does
          not commit you to filing one.
key.l3:
Fault is decided by the insurance companies, not by the police report and not
          at the scene. The report is evidence, not a verdict.
key.l4:
Your deductible comes out of what the carrier pays for your own car. You never
          write anyone a cheque for it.
key.l5:
A rental car is a separate coverage. Plenty of people find out they do not have
          it on the day they need it.

steps.h2: What happens in the first 48 hours
steps.p:
A claim is a sequence, and almost all of the frustration people have with one
        comes from not knowing which step they are on. Here is the whole thing.

s1.p:
By phone or online. You give the date, the location, who was driving, who else
            was involved, and what was damaged. This takes ten to twenty minutes and it is
            the only step where you do all the talking.

s2.p:
Immediately, before the call ends. Write it down. Every conversation about
            this claim from here on starts with that number, and it is not the same as your
            policy number.

s3.p:
Usually within one business day. This is the person who decides what the
            carrier pays. They will call you; if two days pass and nobody has, that is the
            moment to call us rather than to wait politely.

s4.p:
A shop estimate, a drive-in inspection, or photos you take on your phone
            through the carrier's app. Photo estimates are fastest and are now the default
            at most companies for anything that is not severe.

s5.p:
The adjusters at each company compare statements, photos, the police report
            and sometimes the damage patterns. This is the step that takes the longest and
            the one you have the least control over.

s6.p:
Either to the repair shop directly or to you, minus your deductible. If the
            car is financed, the lienholder is usually on the cheque as well — that is
            normal and it is why some payments take an extra week.

steps.p2:
A straightforward claim with clear fault and moderate damage closes in roughly two
        to four weeks. A disputed-fault claim with injuries can run for months. Neither is a
        sign that something has gone wrong.

fault.h2: Who actually decides whose fault it was
fault.p1:
Not the police. This surprises people, and it is the single most common
        misunderstanding we hear.
fault.p2:
A police officer at the scene writes down what they observed and sometimes issues
        a citation. That report is strong evidence and adjusters read it carefully. But the
        decision about who pays is made by the insurance companies involved, comparing what
        each driver said, the physical damage, any photos, any witnesses, and the traffic
        law that applies. An officer can decline to assign fault entirely, and often does.
fault.p3:
Both Texas and New Mexico apportion fault by percentage rather than treating it as
        all-or-nothing, so an outcome like 70/30 is completely normal and changes what each
        side pays. If you are told you were partly at fault and you disagree, say so in
        writing and tell us — that decision can be reconsidered, and it is much easier to
        challenge in week one than in month three.

call.b: Never guess at fault at the scene.
call.p:
"I'm so sorry, I didn't see you" is a human thing to say and it ends up in an
          adjuster's file as an admission. Exchange information, take photographs, be
          decent to the other driver, and let the two companies work out the percentages.
          That is literally what they are for.

ded.p1: The deductible is the part of your own car's repair you absorb. It applies to comprehensive and collision — the coverages that fix your vehicle — and it never applies to what you cause to someone else.

est.span: What the shop says it costs

ded.p2:
The carrier pays $2,700. You pay $500, directly to the
        repair shop, when you collect the car. Nobody sends you a bill for it and it is not
        added to your premium.
ded.p3: Two things worth knowing. First, it applies every time you claim, not once a year. Second, if the other driver is found at fault, their insurer usually reimburses it — a process called subrogation, which happens quietly in the background and can take a few months. You get a cheque you were not expecting, and it is yours.
ded.h3: When a claim is not worth making
ded.p4:
If the repair is $700 and your deductible is $500, you are claiming $200 and
        putting a claim on your record to get it. That is often a bad trade. If the repair
        is $4,000, it obviously is not. In between it depends on your record, your carrier
        and how close you are to renewal — call us and we will work it out with you before
        you file, which is the only useful time to have that conversation.

total.h2: When the car is a total loss
total.p1:
A car is "totalled" when repairing it costs more than a set percentage of what it
        was worth — the threshold varies by carrier and by state, and it is lower than most
        people expect. A ten-year-old car with $6,000 of damage is very often a total loss
        even though it looks fixable.
total.p2: What you are paid is the actual cash value: what your car was worth the moment before the crash, not what you paid for it and not what it costs to replace with a new one. The carrier builds that figure from comparable local sales. You are allowed to disagree with it, and you should if the comparables are wrong — a lower-mileage car, recent tyres, a trim level they missed. Send evidence rather than an opinion.

own.b: If you own the car outright
own.l2: You hand over the title and usually the keys.
own.l3:
Sales tax and title fees are often included — ask, because carriers do not
              always volunteer it.

fin.b: If the car is financed or leased
fin.l1: The lender is paid first, and the cheque names them too.
fin.l2:
If you owe more than the car was worth, you owe the difference — unless
              you carry gap coverage.
fin.l3:
Gap is cheap and most people do not have it. Ask us before you need it,
              not after.

wait.h2: What your policy will and will not do while you wait

rental.p:
Only if you carry rental reimbursement, and only on a covered claim. It pays a
        fixed amount per day — $30, $50, whatever you chose — and anything the rental
        company charges above that is yours. If the other driver is at fault, their liability
        coverage should pay for your rental instead, but that only starts once their carrier
        accepts fault, which can be a week or three.

tow.p:
Storage yards charge by the day and those charges are real money. Tell the adjuster
        immediately where the car is. A vehicle sitting in a lot while nobody knows to move
        it is one of the few ways a claim quietly costs you more than it should.

med.p:
Medical Payments or Personal Injury Protection pay for you and your passengers
        regardless of fault, with no deductible, and they pay quickly. They are the coverages
        people most often decline to save a few dollars and most often wish they had. If you
        do not know whether you carry them, we can tell you in a minute.

rate.p1: Sometimes. Anyone who tells you otherwise before the claim is decided is guessing.
rate.p2:
What actually drives it: whether you were at fault, what the claim cost, what else
        is on your record, and which carrier you are with — companies weigh the same claim
        very differently. A not-at-fault claim can still move a rate at some carriers and
        not at others, which is unsatisfying and true.
rate.p3:
Here is the part that matters and that a direct insurer will not tell you: if your
        rate does move at renewal, that is the moment to re-shop it. We hold appointments
        with more than a dozen companies, and the one that penalises your claim hardest is
        rarely the one that would write you today. That is the whole reason to use an
        independent agent rather than a website with a lizard on it.

call.b: Do not cancel a policy in the middle of an open claim.
call.p:
The claim stays with the carrier that had the policy on the date of the crash —
          cancelling does not make it go away, and it can complicate the payout while
          leaving you with a gap in coverage that raises your next price. Wait for renewal.
          Then let us shop it.

mist.h2: Five mistakes that make a claim harder

m1.b: Waiting to see if the other driver "handles it privately"
m1.p:
People agree to pay cash at the scene and then stop answering the phone. By
            the time you report it, the evidence is gone and your own carrier is hearing
            about it late. Report it. You can always decide not to claim.

m2.b: Not photographing the other insurance card
m2.p:
A name and a phone number is not enough to open a claim against someone. The
            company name and policy number are.

m3.b: Getting the car repaired before it is inspected
m3.p:
The adjuster has to see the damage or the estimate. Fixing it first can leave
            the carrier with nothing to pay against.

m4.p:
You will be asked how fast you were going and how far away the other car was.
            "I don't know" is a complete and acceptable answer. An invented number becomes a
            fact in the file.

m5.p:
Claims stall when nobody chases them. If a week passes with no word, someone
            should call — and that someone can be us.

we.h2: What we do that the carrier does not
we.p1:
Safe House is your agent, not your insurer. We do not decide the claim and we do
        not pay it — the carrier does both. What we do is make sure it is reported the way
        it should be, tell you in plain language what the adjuster just said, chase it when
        it goes quiet, read your declarations page back to you so you know what you actually
        have, and re-shop the policy at renewal if the claim moves your price.
we.p2:
None of that costs anything extra. It is what the commission on the policy is for,
        and it is the reason to have an agent at all.

w1.b: We can report it with you on the line
w1.s:
Three-way with the carrier, so nothing gets said wrong and you are not
            doing it alone from a roadside.

w2.b: We tell you what is on your policy before you decide
w2.s: Deductible, rental, medical, whether a claim is even worth filing.

w3.s:
An agent calling on your behalf gets returned faster than a customer
            calling for the fourth time. That is not fair, and it is true.

w4.s:
More than a dozen companies. The one that punished your claim is rarely
            the cheapest one for you now.

cta.p:
Call us and a licensed bilingual agent will start the claim with you — or go
        straight to your company’s claims line. Both are on the claims page.
